items.body: There are milestones that "normal" children reach within a fairly accurate range. This is absolutely not one of them. It is very much child-dependent.

Is it possible your question could be restated as "when will our son be able to sleep without us rocking him to sleep?"  If so, that's an easier question to answer, because changing a bedtime routine is a common parenting challenge.

By developing an association between you rocking the child to sleep and the act of the child falling asleep, you decrease the likelihood of your child learning how to self-soothe and thus falling asleep independently. I don't know the answer to your question. But it seems to me that rocking the child to sleep is not neutral, it is very much contrary to the concept of sleep training. FWIW, I have seen very poor sleep habits and lack of independent falling asleep in children up to 3 years old, and in one case, 11 years old. As @anongoodnurse mentioned, this is very child-dependent.

In addition to what the others say, in my experience falling asleep without your presence does not have to be a one-time event (as in, once your child does it, they will keep doing it for the rest of their lives). It can also go back and forth, with months of independent sleeping followed by months that your presence is needed.

For us it was a step by step thing. Being carried until at sleep - simple lay down together in the same place until sleep (is not co sleeping for the whole night) - start going a little earlier, with promise to come back in a minute (i.e. to prepare the warm-up-stuffed-toy) and building trust by really coming back! - stay a little longer (i.e. need to do stuff like clean kitchen after dinner) ... It works better or not on a daily basis, as me too as adult feel some days more powerful than others.

Perhaps ask Amazon and Walmart about their storage processes.

There's a contact number for your product's information. Spoil is a vague term, and it implies the product is unusabie, which is often not the case with this kind of problem, but it's a possibility. if the effect of high temperatures is significant (spoilage or loss of significant amount of nutritional value), they can answer that.

@anongoodnurse: it's highly unlikely that the company would state anything other than "product should only be used as specified on the label". Typically environmental requirements are set upfront and all subsequent development and testing is done to this target. That's the only storage temperature against which the product is fully tested and certified (which costs a lot of time and money). Even if they are reasonably sure that it's "perfectly fine at 105F for a few days", they could never say that in public: it would create a massive legal exposure risk.

@Hilmar - It's not as cut and dry as you think. There are many, many products that are fine well after their expiration dates, for example. This is especially true of food items. I have not as much doubt as you do about contacting the manufacturer. What's the harm in trying?

Is there any way we can prevent him from tipping his table over during his meal" I just want to point out here that these two things do not mean the same thing, and can even be polar opposites. Teaching a certain behavior tends to require having them be able to make the "bad" decision so that they learn to not do it even though they could. For most of human history people didn't have the means to easily blend or process their food. One could argue that baby led weaning - just giving your kids cooked, soft foods is the more natural way to teach them to eat.  Focusing on purees likely has more to do with paranoia over choking, than any type of meaningful science.

@mcraenich That's true, but I think, before mixer was invented, babies were breasted longer too. In my grandma's generation, their babies were breastfed until 3-4 y/o. Afaik it's only recently that a one-year-old baby is expected to eat the same things as other (adult) family members (cmiiw).

Back then breast-milk was an excellent source of nutrition in lieu of quality nutrition in the environment, so if it was cheap and available it would make sense to do it longer (and some people still do it for a longer period of time). But kids develop teeth at a young age for a reason, because they need to learn to eat solid food and eventually 'wean' off of milk. Pediatricians wouldn't recommend giving up breast milk or formula before age 1, but after that it's not a big issue nutritionally, if their diet is otherwise fine.

Do you happen to have a source for these guidelines that do not seem reasonable?  It has been awhile since I prepared food for a 1 year old, but I recall most of their meals still being fairly mushy, or at least fairly small in size and easy to break apart with their tongue. Not just 'what the family is having no modifications' as you're implying.
@Zibbobz in the first comment I mentioned 'giving your kids cooked, soft foods'. I'm recommending standard baby-led weaning.
Sorry for not being clear, my comment is directed at @ShaNon the question asker, not your recommendations for feeding.

@Zibbobz I have them in German. It doesn't say giving babies steak or the likes, but in my parents' time it was just still unthinkable to give babies soft food that they had to swallow whole (like, soft broccoli). Usually everything was blended until the baby had enough teeth to chew properly.

@ShaNon babies' gums are fairly hard; they are capable of "gumming" soft foods (instead of chewing them). They don't actually swallow food whole, they kind of mash them with their gums (and possibly tongue). So this only works on foods soft enough to get mashed like that.

As an aside, different things work for different babies. My baby (8 months) won't eat from a spoon I am holding, and isn't quite capable of eating with a spoon herself. She insists on feeding herself, so I put small pieces of sweet potato or banana on her tray, and she can pick them up and eat them. Some babies do much better with purees and gag on anything with texture. It really depends on the baby.

You may be disappointed, but in a case as complex and long-running as yours (and we feel with you), any “quick fix” or experimental half-answer has a high chance of causing even more damage to your child. I agree with previous comments, you and your family need a significant amount of effort for lasting changes. See what you have accomplished already, and nothing happened overnight. It’s a process and with a situation as complex as this, it’s pretty much impossible to sum up all relevant bits in one question, then answer in this format. In short, it’s because we care, not because we don’t.

Great answers, but I would just add - especially at this early an age - that children are unpredictable. When children are older they'll normally accept some time where they're by themselves and parents are in another room, but early on they will need constant attention, as well as their parents to drop everything at a moment's notice. That is a contributing factor in why parents are so busy - the child takes precedence over everything. If you want to talk to your friend, you'll have to try and schedule a time - but be prepared for it not to work or for her to suddenly have to leave.

For reliably killing bacteria, the water needs to be significantly hotter than 50°C. You should have used a temperature in the order of 90 to 100°C (actual boiling water). That is also what the answer by @j4nd3r53n suggests.
@Bart van Ingen Schenau Can you link to a source indicating my PUL pocket diapers can withstand the temperatures you suggest? j4nd3r53n acknowledged boiling water is appropriate for cotton.
@Kilobyte, here is a source: community.babycenter.com/post/a43605667/…. We would normally wash our diapers at 60C and occasionally at 90C.

@Bart van Ingen Schenau I don't see how the source you linked, which is a post and comments from 2013, shows that PUL pocket diapers can withstand 90 to 100°C. One comment claims PUL can be boiled, while a friend of mine claims the opposite. Neither provided evidence to back their claims. Have you a reliable source?

Have you asked your pediatrician if what you're doing is good for the child? The pediatrician knows the child and knows if the child has special requirements. Not knowing the child's past medical history and possible problems, it's hard to suggest anything different than what your pediatrician has suggested. Why are you not using formula as the base for a smoothie? Also, if you disagree with the pediatrician, is it possible to get a seconf opinion?  All these questions matter.

Can you notice it ahead? If so, would some comforting while she's just asleep help? My kid sometimes has a nightmare, when we're at it quick enough and give him a slow, light, comforting backrub he often calms down.

Does the child really wake up or do they scream in their sleep ? I am verifying, since there is a difference between nightmares and night terrors - both may emerge at this age. Nightmares are more likely in the morning, since they occur in the light phase of sleep, while the terrors take place in deep sleep.
